title: One fret, one half step
summary: Every interval on the guitar is a fret count. Learn the count once and you stop memorizing shapes — you start deriving them.

body.body: A **half step** is the smallest distance Western music uses. On a piano it is any two keys that touch — including the two white pairs with no black key between them. That exception is the only thing that makes the keyboard awkward to count on.

body.caption: E→F and B→C are half steps with no black key between them. Every other white pair is a whole step.

body.body: The guitar has no such exception. **One fret is one half step, everywhere, on every string.** Walk up the low E and you get all twelve notes in order, then E again.

body.caption: The low E string, nut to 12th fret. Sharps are faded so the natural notes read as the landmarks they are.

body.body: Notice E→F is one fret and B→C is one fret, same as the keyboard. The guitar does not hide the exception — it just stops making it look special.

body.text: Every interval is a fret count

body.body: An interval name is a label for a number of half steps. On the guitar that number *is* a number of frets, so the names below are directly playable on one string.

body.caption: Counting up from an open low E.

body.body: The major scale picks seven of those thirteen. In degree terms:
Which comes out as the fret pattern **2 – 2 – 1 – 2 – 2 – 2 – 1**: two frets, two frets, one, two, two, two, one. That sequence is the major scale. Everything else in this lesson follows from it.

body.title: Name frets, don't find them
body.body: Pick a random fret on the low E and name it *before* you play it, by counting up from the open string. Slow is fine. You are building the count, not the recall.

body.title: Play intervals from one anchor
body.body: Hold fret 5 (A) as your root. Play a major 3rd (4 frets up, fret 9), then a perfect 5th (7 up, fret 12). Sing each one. The sound and the fret count should start arriving together.

body.title: Cross to the A string
body.body: The A string is a perfect 4th above E — 5 half steps. So any fret on E is the same note as *five frets lower* on A, one string up. You just derived the tuning instead of memorizing it.

body.text: Why chord shapes look the way they do

body.body: A major triad is root, major 3rd, perfect 5th — 0, 4, 7 half steps. A minor triad flattens the third to 3. **One half step is the entire difference**, and on the neck that is one fret.

body.caption: Major triad. The third is 4 half steps above the root in pitch, but sits on the next string up — and that string change already accounts for 5 frets, which is why its dot looks lower on the neck.
Minor triad. Identical shape, third moved down exactly one fret: 3 half steps instead of 4. That one fret is the whole major/minor distinction.

body.body: Change the root above and both shapes move together, keeping their fret counts. That is the whole reason guitarists talk in shapes: the counts are fixed, so the shape is portable.
